RagShortTexts: Universities climbed the seven liberal arts, applying scholastic disputatio to harmonize.

Variants.Content: University lectures in Paris, Bologna and Oxford centred on the seven liberal arts. The Trivium of grammar, rhetoric and logic came first, and the Quadrivium of arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy followed for students who had mastered the basics. Teaching reached its peak in the scholastic disputation, a formal contest in which a master set a question, students argued each side, and the master gave a final ruling. Masters tried to reconcile the authority of the Church Fathers with the newly translated works of Aristotle, which reached Latin readers through Arabic and Greek sources. Thomas Aquinas drew the sharpest debates of the period, since his synthesis of Aristotelian logic and Christian doctrine raised questions that many masters had never faced before.

Autonomous guilds of masters and students held papal charters exempting them from municipal bailiffs. Disputes between Dominican Thomists and Averroist philosophers sparked fiery campus controversies.
Pauper clerks sit on straw-strewn floors copying glosses onto costly vellum folios. Earning a master's hood transforms even a yeoman's son into a royal chancellor or ecclesiastical advocate.
